You don't need a perfect plan. You need one thing shipped today: a dashboard, a site, a DM, a call. Stack those and the plan writes itself.
Nobody in your town is faster than you at building AI tools. A business owner who sees a working demo in 48 hours doesn't shop around.
You control messages sent and calls booked. You don't control who says yes. Track the first, and the second takes care of itself.
Your first client is a learning fee
Charge, but don't overthink the price on client one. The case study it gives you is worth more than the retainer.
Every 'no' tells you something: wrong niche, wrong offer, wrong message, or wrong timing. Write down which one and fix it before the next 20.
The students who land clients fastest start outreach in week one with a half-built demo. Readiness comes from reps, not from more videos.
Points for daily activity are small on purpose. The habit is the point. Log in, do one thing, keep the streak alive.
Post what you're building, even if it's ugly. Business owners buy from people who look busy and competent, and nothing says that like progress posts.
If you're not where you want to be on it, look at your outreach count. It's almost always the gap.
One tool you actually use beats ten you've signed up for. Pick Base44 plus one outreach channel and go deep.
Treat coaching calls like client meetings
Show up with your screen ready, a specific question, and your numbers. You'll get ten times more out of Adriel and Jake.
Being the AI guy for dentists in one city beats being the AI guy for everyone, everywhere. Specificity sells.
Pick a niche that already spends
Look for businesses that already pay for ads, software, or lead gen. If they're spending, they understand ROI and your pitch is easier.
Do they have money? Do they have a painful, obvious problem? Can you reach the owner directly? Two out of three isn't enough.
Sell the outcome, not the tool
Nobody wants 'an AI agent.' They want more booked appointments, fewer missed calls, faster quotes. Lead with the result.
One offer, one price, one page
If your offer takes more than two sentences to explain, simplify it. Clear beats clever every time.
Look at what they're already paying for
If a med spa pays $800/month for a booking tool and $1,500 for an agency, a $1,000 AI system that does both is an easy yes.
Read Google reviews and Facebook groups in your niche. The exact complaints customers write are your ad copy and your pitch.
Local businesses answer the phone, meet in person, and refer each other. Start within driving distance. Scale out later.
Don't guarantee revenue. Guarantee speed ('live in 7 days') or effort ('we rebuild it free until it works'). Risk reversal that doesn't bankrupt you.
Price for the problem, not your hours
A tool that saves a roofer two lost jobs a month is worth $1,000+ regardless of whether it took you a weekend to build.
One slide: what their business looks like today, what it looks like with your system. Use it in every pitch.
Avoid niches that argue about price
Restaurants and nail salons are tough. Contractors, dentists, lawyers, gyms, and med spas have margin and understand marketing.
'The Lead Rescue System' sounds like a product. 'An AI chatbot' sounds like a commodity. Naming it lets you set the price.
Scrape their site, grab their services, use their logo. A demo built for them converts five times better than a generic one.
Start from a template, not a blank screen
In Base44, clone something that works and change the copy and colors. First versions should take an hour, not a day.
A working dashboard with a plain layout beats a beautiful mockup that doesn't work. Owners care if it functions, not if it's pretty.
Build the demo before the call
Walk into every discovery call with something to show. 'Here's what I already built for you' changes the whole conversation.
Super agents that try to do everything break. Build an agent that handles one thing perfectly (missed-call texts, quote follow-ups) and add from there.
Before you show a client, go through the whole flow on your phone as if you were their customer. Fix every friction point you hit.
Record a 2-minute Loom of every build
Walk through the dashboard on video. Send it instead of a long email. Prospects watch videos; they skim emails.
Connect the dashboard to something they already check
Owners live in their phone and their calendar. If your system texts them or drops into their calendar, they'll actually use it.
Every build goes on one page with a screenshot and a one-line result. Link it in your bio and your outreach.
Your second client in the same niche should take a third of the time. Save your prompts, layouts, and automations as templates.
Use Claude to write the copy
Ask it for headlines, service descriptions, and FAQ answers in the client's voice. Edit, don't start from zero.
An AI receptionist that answers in the owner's name, a dashboard that shows revenue in real time. One feature they'll show their friends.
Judging a message after three sends is noise. Send twenty, then look at replies and adjust.
Lead with their problem, not your pitch
'Noticed your site doesn't let people book online. Built a quick fix for you, want to see it?' beats any intro about yourself.
A 45-second screen recording of their website with your suggestions gets replies where text gets ignored.
Most replies come on follow-up three or four. Space them out: day 1, 3, 7, 14, 30. Keep each one short and useful.
Owners of local businesses answer their own phones before the day gets busy. Afternoons go to voicemail.
For local niches, nothing beats showing up with a tablet and a demo. Ten walk-ins a week will book more than 200 cold emails.
Ask for the referral on day one
'Who else do you know with the same problem?' right after they say yes. Warm intros close at three times the rate.
Log every message, call, and DM in the Achievements tab. What gets measured gets done, and the badges unlock on their own.
Keep the first message under 50 words
Owners read on their phone. If it needs scrolling, it doesn't get read.
Spend two days engaging with a prospect's posts. Your DM lands as a familiar name instead of a stranger.
Don't outreach from memory. Spreadsheet with name, business, phone, Instagram, status. Work the list top to bottom.
Post a case study every week
Even a small one. 'Built this for a local gym in 2 days, booked 11 trials in the first week.' Inbound starts when people see results.
Each ad makes one clear promise to one type of customer. Trying to say everything is how ads get ignored.
If the first line doesn't name the viewer's problem or desire, they scroll. Write ten hooks, test the best three.
Script with AI, film with your phone
Use the ad scripting module to generate the structure, then record it yourself. Real beats polished for local businesses.
Meta Ads Library and the Google Transparency Center show what competitors have been running for months. Long-running ads are working ads.
Let an ad run 3 days before judging
Meta needs time to learn. Killing ads after 24 hours wastes every dollar you spent on them.
The cheapest conversions are people who already looked. Set up a retargeting audience before you run cold traffic.
Targeting matters less every year. Spend your time on the hook, the visual, and the offer, not on interest stacks.
A 15-second testimonial from a client is the best ad you'll ever run for your own agency.
Owners don't care about CPM. Show them leads, cost per lead, and booked appointments. Everything else is noise to them.
Build the system first, then say 'want me to send traffic to it?' Ads become a second retainer, not a harder first sale.
Ad fatigue is real. Rotate new hooks and visuals before results drop, not after.
Keep the landing page to one action
One headline, one offer, one button. Every extra link is a leak.
Ask about the problem for 10 minutes before pitching
The best closers talk 30% of the time. Let the owner describe their pain in their own words, then reflect it back.
Share your screen and click through the demo. Owners decide in the first 60 seconds of seeing something real.
Anchor to what they already spend
'You're paying $2,000 a month for an answering service that misses calls. This is $800 and never sleeps.'
A $750 setup plus $500/month and a $1,500 all-in. People pick between options more easily than they say yes or no to one.
Handle 'let me think about it' with a question
'Totally fair. What's the part you want to think through?' Nine times out of ten it's price or trust, and both are answerable.
Send the Stripe link on the call
If they say yes, take payment while you're still talking. 'I'll send the invoice later' loses a third of deals.
Set the next step before hanging up
Onboarding call booked, logins requested, start date agreed. No call ends without a calendar event.
Setup fee plus monthly retainer. The setup fee pays you for the build; the retainer builds the business.
Say the number, then stop talking. The first person to speak after the price is quoted usually loses.
Listen back to one call a week. You'll hear yourself over-explaining or skipping the ask. Nothing improves closing faster.
Short calls get accepted. Owners say no to 'a quick hour' and yes to 'twenty minutes to show you what I built.'
The proposal is a recap, not a pitch
If you need a proposal to convince them, the call wasn't done. The proposal should just confirm what you both agreed.
A single 45-minute call: logins, phone number, calendar, go live. Drag it out over weeks and the client cools off.
Every Friday: 'Here's what the system did this week. Here's what I'm improving next.' Clients who hear from you don't churn.
Document every step of your build and onboarding. When it's a checklist, you can hand it to someone else.
If your last three signed without pushback, your price is too low. Add 20% for the next one.
Collect the testimonial at the first win
Ask the day they tell you about a result, not six months later. A text with a screenshot is enough.
Three clients in one niche, then move
Three gives you a repeatable build, a case study, and referrals. Then either go deeper or add a second niche.
You teach clients to follow up automatically. Do the same for your pipeline. Your own GHL should chase your leads.
Check in on the Recordings page
Missed a call? The replay is there. The best questions from other students are usually the ones you'd have asked.
Track monthly recurring revenue, not deals
A $500/month client is worth $6,000 a year. Build the business around retainers and the math gets fun fast.
Stack systems for the same client
Dashboard, then AI receptionist, then ads, then a review engine. Four retainers from one client who already trusts you.
Don't abandon a client for a shiny niche
Your current clients are the easiest revenue you'll ever get. Expand what you do for them before chasing new ones.
